# Get the population data you need

`tarr.pop` helps you retrieve population counts for selected places, years, and demographic groups.
You can return those counts as a data frame or tibble for analysis, reporting, or plotting. This
guide uses an example for obtaining population estimates for Dallas and Tarrant counties for
2015–2018 using the abbreviated population cube included with the package.

Population data when represented as a data frame are very convenient for grouping, sub-setting,
aggregating, joining, etc . However, reading large population data sets into R can be memory
intensive, using tens or even hundreds of megabytes of memory. The tarr.pop package enables efficient 
population retrieval by two means: efficient data organization with persistent storage on
disk and manipulation of metadata that reduces the data items for loading into memory.

Two terms you need to know to understand how the package functions works - delayed and eager. You
will often see the term "lazy" which is just another way to say "delayed". Lazy functions store
steps in memory and do not execute until the data from disk is needed. The eager functions cause the in-memory steps 
to be 'realozed' and fetch only the selected needed data from disk.

Traditionally population data is represented as a data frame with many repeating values. Below in the left column is part of an example data frame. Note how many values in each column are repeated.  A multi-dimensional array of the same data is represented on the right. Each array dimension cateogry is stored only once.  

::: {.columns}
 
::: {.column width="55%"}
 
### Data Frame
 
| year | county | sex | age | race.eth | population |
|:-----|:-------|:-------|----:|:---------|-----------:|
| 2017 | Tarrant | female | 22 | asian | 796 |
| 2017 | Tarrant | male | 22 | asian | 914 |
| 2017 | Tarrant | female | 23 | asian | 876 |
| 2017 | Tarrant | male | 23 | asian | 947 |
| 2017 | Tarrant | female | 24 | asian | 1002 |
| 2017 | Tarrant | male | 24 | asian | 1049 |
 
:::
 
::: {.column width="45%"}
 
### Multidimensional Array
 
```text
year = 2017
county = Tarrant
race.eth = asian
 
        age
sex       22   23   24
  female 796  876 1002
  male   914  947 1049
```
 
:::

:::
 
### Multidimensional Array
 
[Arrays](https://www.programiz.com/r/arrays) store data much more efficiently than data frames. Each dimension
categories or levels are only stored once. For population stratified by age, sex, race, ethnicity, area, and year, an
array can be 20% of the data frame size. The second part is manipulating the metadata with delayed or lazy computation.
For example, selecting the years, ages, county you want, then aggregating by one or more groups are all done in memory
without touching the numeric data on disk. Then when you want the data you use a function that eagerly fetches the data
and any delayed actions are 'realized'. Only selected data is retrieved from disk, and the manipulations tht were
delayed are "realized". This workflow reduces memory use by reading only selected data and saves execution time through
delayed execution optimization.

Arrays can have multiple dimensions. Think of as a 2-dimension array as a table with rows and columns. A 3-dimension
array is a cube with rows, columns and depth. An array with more than three dimensions is hard to visualize in a
physical sense, but can be thought of as a "hyper-cube". For simplicity, the package refers to all population arrays
with multiple dimensions as population arrays or cubes. The object you create when opening a population cube is called a
`poparray`.

To retrieve population data, open a population cube (`open_poparry()`), inspect its labels and
categories (`dimnames() and dim_labels()`), select the population you need
(`filter() and the [] operator`), and convert the result to a table/data frame
(`as.data.frame(), as_tibble(), or as.array()`). Some of the dplyr functions that is often used to
lazily manipulate the meta-data. Those are `filter()`, `rename`, `relocate`, and `select()`.

Dimension levels can be grouped or "collapsed"  
(`collapse_dim(), collapse_all(), group_ages()`) into fewer groups within the dimension.  This will cause an
automatic sum of the population figures for the new groupings. All this is done by manipulating
the metadata - dimension selection, removing or grouping categories, then converting to a data.frame
or an in-memory array which causes only the desired data to be fetched from disk.

A population array/cube contains two or more dimensions and is saved to disk in a compressed
[HDF5](https://support.hdfgroup.org/documentation/hdf5/latest/_intro_h_d_f5.html) type file. The
dimensions and categories/levels contained in them are used to select the data that you may need.
For example a cell might contain the number of female residents of Tarrant County aged 65 in 2018 in
a particular race/ethnicity category. The dimension labels identify which population each count
describes. The package keeps that structure and its metadata together while you select and summarize
data.

# Find and open a cube

The main function for opening a population array is pop_array(). You pass the file name complete
with the file path, or use the tarr.pop named list `pop_catalog` to select the name of the
population cube of interest. The catalog is organized first by source agency of the data - U.S.
Census Bureau, Texas Demographic Center, and the National Cancer Institute SEER program. Each source
agency can have more than one population cube. For example pop_catalog\$census.bureau has references
population cubes containing Texas county decennial census counts, county estimates, and Tarrant
County ZCTA estimates with margins of error.

## Load the bundled example

The package includes a small TDC county population estimates cube that will be used in the following
examples.

```{r libraries}
#| message: false
library(tarr.pop)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
```

Using `system.file()` to find the example data inside the installed tarr.pop package, then pass its
path to `open_poparray()`:

```{r open_tdc_estimates}
example_path <-  system.file("extdata/tdc_example.h5", package = "tarr.pop")
stopifnot(nzchar(example_path))
pop <- open_poparray(filepath = example_path)
pop
```

Opening reads the labels and metadata and creates a disk-backed view. It does not load every
population value into memory. Rather all the meta data is loaded so you can select what may be
needed, then "realize" the data when the `poparray` is converted using a function like
as.data.frame() or as_tibble(). The open_poparray() function returns an object of type `poparray`.
You can get a summary of the returned poparray by typing its name and running that one line. THe
summary as given here gives some source information, the last time it was updated to disk, length is
the number of data elements in the poparray, the names of the dimensions that are used for the time
and area roles, then a list of all the dimensions and all the levels/categories contained in each
dimension.\
This example population cube contains Collin, Dallas, Denton, and Tarrant counties estimates for the
years 2015–2018 by sex, age, and race/ethnicity.

The example below selects Tarrant and Dallas counties that will be used for later comparison. The
TDC uses one combined `race.eth` dimension for race and Hispanic ethnicity. Other sources may use
separate dimensions, so always inspect the cube you open.

## Inspect coverage and labels

Start with the source notes and available dimensions. These operations inspect metadata without
extracting population values.

```{r inspect_cube}
source_meta(pop)  # Show the genera meta data 
dimnames(pop) |> names()  # Names of each dimension
dim(pop) # The number of categories/levels in each dimension. 

# Explore levels or categories for several dimensions
# 
# dim_labels() is the function you can use with any dimension name
dim_labels(pop, "race.eth")

# Look at the labels in each dimension
# These convenience functions are wrappers around dim_labels()
times(pop) |> head()
areas(pop) |> head()
ages(pop)  |> head()
sexes(pop)
```

`times()` and `areas()` return the labels for the time and area roles. `ages()` and `sexes()` are
convenient ways to inspect demographic labels. These are just function wrappers around the
dim_labels() function. Use `dim_labels()` for any named dimension, such as `race.eth`. The
dimensions here are `year`, `area.name`, `sex`, `age.char`, and `race.eth`. When a

## Handle the 2016–2017 category changes

A **schema** is the set of categories used to report the data. The TDC changed both age and race/ethnicity categories in
2017. Through 2016, age ended with `"85 +"` (everyone aged 85 or older). From 2017 on, ages 85–94 are reported
individually, followed by `"95 +"`. Asian residents were included in `"other"` through 2016 and reported separately as
`"asian"` from 2017.

The cube contains the combined list of labels from both periods. That does not mean every label applies in every year.
For example, the absence of a separate Asian count in 2016 does not mean there were no Asian residents, they were just
included in the "other" category. Likewise, removing `"85 +"` from all years would remove the older population from 2015
and 2016.

The example cube includes **applicability** metadata for the TDC reporting periods. This records which age and
race/ethnicity categories apply in each year. The package uses this metadata to sum the appropriate categories for each
year while keeping genuinely missing counts as missing. 

## Select your population

Suppose we want Dallas and Tarrant counties for years 2016 through 2018. Select places and years
first:

```{r select_counties_and_years}
target_counties <- c("Dallas", "Tarrant")
example_years <- 2016:2018

pop_small <- pop |>
  dplyr::filter(
    area.name %in% target_counties,
    year %in% example_years
  )

pop_small
```

Here, `filter()` selects labels along cube dimensions. It keeps all combinations of the selected
coordinates, For another question, you could also select particular sex, age, or race/ethnicity
labels.

Filtering is "lazy" or a delayed function: it creates a smaller view without extracting the
population values. Compare the number of cells before and after selection.

```{r selection_sizes}
c(original_cells = length(pop), selected_cells = length(pop_small))
```

You now have two choices. Keep the demographic detail if you need one row for each group, or
collapse those dimensions if you need county totals.

# Choose detail or totals, then return a table

## Keep demographic detail

When you want separate demographic groups, convert the filtered cube directly. For example, this
produces a tibble for female residents in Tarrant county by year, retaining age and
race/ethnicity categories:

```{r detailed_table}
selected_groups <- pop_small |>
  dplyr::filter(
    area.name == "Tarrant",
    year == example_years[length(example_years)],
    sex == "female"
  )

# EAGER: read this selected result into memory.
detail_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(selected_groups)
head(detail_tbl)
```

There is one row per selected cube cell, with one column for each dimension and a value column named
`population` in this series. Dimension labels may become factors when converting to a tibble, including ordered factors
for age and time. Missing counts remain missing; an `NA` does not mean zero. Conversion preserves the cube's categories,
so an overlapping category may still appear in this detailed table. Be cautious about summing its rows indiscriminately.

## Calculate county totals safely

For county totals, sum over age, sex, and the combined race/ethnicity classification. First check
whether the selected categories overlap:

```{r inspect_overlap}
overlaps(pop_small)
```

The overlap report lists `"85 +"` because the complete age-label list also includes individual older
ages. With the period metadata above, those labels are never used together in a sum. Keep `"85 +"`
for the earlier years and let `collapse_all()` use each year's applicable labels. There is no need
to remove an age group or turn off the safety checks as the applicability information in the cube will handle it.

Now collapse age, race/ethnicity, and sex which will cause summing of the individual population
entries into thelarger groups.

```{r county_totals}
pop_totals <- pop_small |>
  collapse_all(dim = c("age.char", "race.eth", "sex"))

pop_totals
```

Collapsing reads and sums values in blocks and writes a new HDF5-backed result. It is bounded-memory
computation, rather than another queued filter. The time and area dimensions remain, while each
collapsed dimension has one level called `"all"`.

There is an alternative way to collapse the  age.char, race.eth, and sex dimensions, that is to just select the
dimensions you want to keep. Those dimensions not selected will be automatically collapsed and dropped.  The data in
those dimensions are summed wiht the dimensions you select so no data is lost.

```{r county_totals_2}
pop_totals_2 <- pop_small |> 
  select(year, area.name)

pop_totals_2
```


## Choose a data frame or tibble

Both conversions below are **eager**: they read the selected result into R memory. That is why we
first selected the relevant counties and years and, for totals, collapsed the demographic detail.

```{r convert_totals}
county_df <- as.data.frame(pop_totals)
county_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(pop_totals)
county_tbl
```

Both tables contain the same population values. Choose a data frame for base R tools or a tibble for
a tidyverse workflow. With two counties and three  years, the total table contains eight rows. The
`sex`, `age.char`, and `race.eth` columns contain `"all"`, recording the dimensions that were
summed.

For reporting, keep just the columns you need and convert the year labels to integers. Convert
through character so factor codes are not mistaken for years:

```{r reporting_table}
county_tbl <- county_tbl |>
  dplyr::select(year, area.name, population) |>
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.integer(as.character(year)))

county_tbl
```

At this point you have an ordinary in-memory table. You can join it to other analysis data, write it
to a file, or plot it using your usual R tools.

# Compare age or race groups across the change

County totals are comparable because all residents are included in both periods. For an age-specific
comparison, use a common age grouping. `group_ages()` can retain the earlier `"85 +"` count and sum
the later individual ages 85–94 plus `"95 +"` to obtain the same 85-and-older group:

```{r common_age_groups}
pop_age_groups <- pop_small |>
  group_ages(c("0-84", "85+")) |>
  collapse_all(dim = c("race.eth", "sex"))

# EAGER: read only the small grouped result for display.
age_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(pop_age_groups)
age_tbl
```

The output labels may include spaces, such as `"85 +"`. Age groups are interpreted as intervals, not
by matching their spelling. You cannot recover a separate 90-and-older count for 2015 or 2016 from
the broader 85-and-older count. Requesting such a group produces a warning and `NA` for the years
where it cannot be derived.

For race/ethnicity comparisons, keep the meaning consistent too. One option is to combine `"asian"`
and `"other"` in the later years to match the earlier `"other"` category:

```{r common_race_groups}
pop_race_groups <- pop_small |>
  collapse_dim(
    dim = "race.eth",
    groups = list(
      "Asian and other" = c("asian", "other"),
      "Black" = "black",
      "Hispanic" = "hispanic",
      "White" = "white"
    )
  ) |>
  collapse_all(dim = c("age.char", "sex"))

# EAGER: display the selected, summarized counts.
race_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(pop_race_groups)
race_tbl
```

The period metadata makes the first group use only `"other"` in 2015–2016 and `"asian"` plus
`"other"` in 2017–2018. It cannot split the earlier `"other"` count into its Asian and non-Asian
components. Avoid using `sum(..., na.rm = TRUE)` as a shortcut for handling this change: missing
reporting categories and genuinely missing counts have different meanings.

# Plot the result

```{r plot_totals}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 4.8
ggplot(county_tbl, aes(x = year, y = population, color = area.name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Population estimates for Dallas and Tarrant counties",
    subtitle = paste("Texas Demographic Center;", paste(range(county_tbl$year), collapse = "–")),
    x = "Year",
    y = "Population",
    color = "County"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

# How the package protects your results

The object opened above is a `poparray`. It combines an array of population values with dimension
labels, source notes, time and area roles, and semantic metadata. The DelayedArray backend supports deferred
operations, while HDF5Array provides disk-backed storage. Keeping the large source cube on disk and
extracting only your analysis slice avoids unnecessary memory use.

A dimension's `DimSemantics` metadata describes two separate properties. Its partition type says
whether categories are mutually exclusive or may overlap. Its scale type says how labels should be
interpreted: for example, age groups have interval meaning rather than being arbitrary strings.
Those properties help the package reject unsafe aggregation.

```{r inspect_semantics}
time_role(pop)
area_role(pop)
dim_semantics(pop)$age.char
```

These checks cannot replace understanding the source. TDC's combined race/ethnicity classification is
different from separate race and ethnicity dimensions. Likewise, Census counts, annual estimates,
and projections answer different questions. 

# Where to go next

Use this workflow for your next question: choose the source, inspect its coverage, select your
places and groups, decide whether to retain detail or calculate totals, then convert to a table. Keep
population values on disk until you need them, and review overlap warnings before summing.

For more detail, see the [API reference](api_reference.qmd), the [`poparray` class
guide](poparray_class.Rmd), or the [projection introduction](poparray_projection_intro.Rmd).
Function help such as `?dim_labels`, `?filter.poparray`, and `?collapse_all` provides argument
details and examples.
